extracted.intended_audience: researchers, graduate students, and advanced readers interested in philosophy of mathematics and foundations (set theory, logic, proof theory)
extracted.subtask_description: An overview chapter discussing standards, justificatory criteria, and conceptual desiderata in foundations of mathematics (set theory, large cardinals, categoricity, computability, and mathematical proof). Useful for evaluating positions and arguments in philosophy of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative conception of sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes how the set-theoretical universe can be thought of as generated from the empty set by means of the power set operation (the iterative conception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The iterative conception motivates some axioms of ZFC very well (e.g., the power set axiom) but fares less well with respect to other axioms such as the replacement axiom (Potter 2004, Part IV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of size conception
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that every collection which is not too big to be a set is a set (the limitation of size conception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conception motivates other axioms better (such as the restricted comprehension axiom). The text notes there is no uniform conception that clearly justifies all axioms of ZFC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of proper classes (Cantorian inconsistent multiplicities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantor's recognition that some pluralities are 'too large to be considered as a set' (inconsistent multiplicities), now called proper classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some philosophers treat proper classes as collections (but this faces regress problems: no proper class of all proper classes), while Zermelo argued proper classes do not exist and one need not quantify over them in ZFC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of axioms: intrinsic vs extrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes intrinsic support (e.g., conceptual or reflective grounds) from extrinsic support (e.g., consequences, fruitfulness) for putative axioms beyond ZFC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weaker large cardinal principles are often supported by intrinsic evidence (reflection principles); stronger ones typically enjoy only extrinsic support. The debate concerns whether principles have the right kind of justificatory support to count as basic axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection principles as evidence for large cardinals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection principles state that the set-theoretic universe is so rich that it is very similar to some set-sized initial segment of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflection principles provide intrinsic evidence for some (weaker) large cardinal hypotheses by exhibiting structural similarity between the whole universe and initial segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large cardinal axioms characterized by embedding properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Large cardinals are understood as hypotheses often formulated in terms of embedding properties between the set-theoretic universe and inner models; they typically posit existence of sets larger than those guaranteed by ZFC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text distinguishes weaker large cardinals (intrinsic support) from stronger ones (extrinsic support). Examples: Woodin cardinals yield strong consequences in descriptive set theory and solve restricted definable continuum problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuum hypothesis and independence as a criterion for (un)decidability
rubrics_metrics.description: The continuum hypothesis (CH) is independent of ZFC (Gödel and Cohen); even adding large cardinals does not decide CH in full generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical implications: some think CH is absolutely undecidable (neither true nor false); a multiverse view implies models making CH true and models making it false are equally good, so no unique truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categoricity as a desideratum for fixing intended models
rubrics_metrics.description: If a theory has, up to isomorphism, exactly one model then it is categorical; Dedekind showed arithmetic and real analysis have unique intended models (modulo isomorphism) when treated second-orderly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal to second-order logic is used to obtain categoricity for arithmetic and analysis and quasi-categoricity for set theory; this is important for structuralist projects that want to fix intended models by axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zermelo quasi-categoricity for set theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Zermelo's quasi-categoricity: for any two models M1 and M2 of the principles of set theory, either M1 ≅ M2, or M1 ≅ a strongly inaccessible rank of M2, or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zermelo's result is 'almost' categoricity for set theory; there have been attempts to strengthen it to full categoricity, but the article does not pursue those arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order logic's ontological and set-theoretic entanglements
rubrics_metrics.description: Full second-order logic requires quantifiers ranging over all subsets (or properties), which appears to commit one ontologically to classes and ties second-order logical truths to set-theoretic questions (e.g., continuum hypothesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections: Boolos offered a plural interpretation to avoid class commitment, but Quine-style objections point out that second-order logic is intertwined with deep set-theoretic issues and may inherit indeterminacy from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural interpretation of second-order quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: An interpretation (Boolos) that treats second-order quantification via plural expressions without invoking classes: e.g., 'there are some x such that they have property F'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretation aims to avoid ontological commitment to abstract objects, though it is controversial whether pluralities differ materially from sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quinean objection linking second-order logic to set theory (indeterminacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quine's objection: interpreting full second-order logic connects it with set-theoretical questions (e.g., uses axiom of choice) and certain second-order logical truths are equivalent to set-theoretic propositions like CH, imparting indeterminacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If CH is truth-valueless or undecidable, then some notions about second-order infinite models may also lack determinate truth-values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative methods to ensure categoricity (stronger quantifiers or computability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Options include introducing quantifiers intermediate between first and second order (e.g., 'there are finitely many x') or taking algorithmic computability as primitive to isolate intended models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tennenbaum's theorem shows that first-order nonstandard models of PA with computable operations are isomorphic to the standard model, suggesting computability constraints can pick out intended models; but this approach is limited for real analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal categoricity arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: If two agents regard the collection of predicates for which induction is permissible as open-ended and accept each other's induction schemes, they can be convinced their idiolects describe isomorphic structures (Parsons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'internal' arguments aim to show categoricity without appealing to stronger logic or external primitives; they are widely debated in contemporary literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical pluralism as a thesis about models and theories
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that consistent mathematical theories have many structurally different models and that many or all such models are on a par (no single theory more true than another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roots in Hilbert (consistency suffices) and Carnap (choice between frameworks is pragmatic); the view faces critiques and counterarguments from defenders of uniqueness or realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church's Thesis: status and types of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Church's Thesis: every algorithmically computable function on the natural numbers can be computed by a Turing machine. It links an informal notion (algorithmic computability) to a formal one (Turing computability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its status is curious: almost universally held but hard to prove because of informal antecedent. Evidence is quasi-empirical and extrinsic (equivalence of different formalizations), while Kreisel's 'informal rigour' and Sieg's analysis try to supply intrinsic justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for an informal mathematical proof (received view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Received view: an informal mathematical argument constitutes a proof if it allows a competent mathematician to transform it into a formal deduction of the statement from generally accepted mathematical axioms (the argument is a derivation-indicator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This view faces challenges: interpolating reasons to reach a logically correct first-order derivation may be an infinite process, and there is lively debate about the adequacy of the received view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status and epistemology of computer-assisted proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-assisted proofs (e.g., the four-colour theorem) involve case-checking verified by computers that are too long for humans to check; this raises questions about whether such proofs yield a priori knowledge or are quasi-empirical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments differ: some claim reliance on hardware/software makes acceptance empirical (Tymoczko), others argue the empirical factors don't appear as premises so a priori status can be preserved (Burge), though Burge later revised his view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for a 'good' mathematical proof: explanation and understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond merely showing a statement is true, a 'good' proof should explain why the statement holds by referring to deep relations between deep mathematical concepts and often linking different domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer proofs are often criticised for lacking explanatory depth and for failing to develop or link deep concepts; philosophical investigation into 'mathematical understanding' is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate over the extension and measurability of informal provability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the extension of informal mathematical provability outstrips provability in any given formal system (as Lucas, Penrose argue) or might coincide with some formal system (Benacerraf), and whether the concept is even precise enough to decide enumerability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions vary: arguments that informal provability exceeds any formal system are widely regarded as unpersuasive; others argue the question may be ill-posed due to indeterminacy of 'informal provability'.
